In the early 18th century, European architecture was an elaborately decorated wall architecture featuring thick, high stone walls to express spiritual and religious authority. It heavily relied on intricate ornamental details and massive stonework. In this approach, structural efficiency and the rational use of materials were largely (a) ignored to achieve dramatic visual impact. However, by the mid-18th century, some scholars opposed this tradition by promoting the noble simplicity, which eliminated excess ornament in favor of structural economy. They argued that true architectural beauty lies in structural honesty and functional simplicity rather than heavy decoration. In this climate, a young generation of architects with engineering backgrounds viewed its thick walls and excessive details as a (b) waste of materials from a structural engineering perspective. Enlightened priests seeking a rational reinterpretation of religious teachings shared this view, asserting that architecture should (c) take the fundamental form ― a primitive hut made only of columns and a roof, free from unnecessary walls. Even so, they wished to preserve the divinity unique to religious architecture. They, thus, did not completely (d) include the overwhelming physical presence and dramatic visual impact of the earlier tradition. This (e) reconciliation generated a new design ideal that unified the structural logic of column-based forms with the sacred, luminous height of traditional religious architecture.

(A)
The wind was blowing strongly as Elias stood by the open door of the plane. His blond hair moved wildly. “Ready to jump, Elias?” Gustav, his skydiving instructor, asked. Elias took a deep breath. “Not really,” (a) he said, holding tightly to the sides of the doorway. It was his first real jump after completing his training, and he was more nervous than he had expected. Elias looked down at the Alps far below. The snowy mountains looked beautiful in the sunlight. He closed his eyes and tried to calm himself down.

(B)
The two were now falling quickly through the air. At first, Elias had trouble controlling his body in the strong wind. Gustav stayed close to Elias, watching (b) him carefully and helping him keep the right position as they fell. After a few moments, Elias was able to look around. The beautiful white mountains spread out below him. The view was so different from anything he had ever seen before. Elias gradually began to enjoy the experience.

(C)
When Elias opened his eyes, his fear returned. “I think I’d rather stay on the plane,” he said. “Come on, you’ll be fine. Just remember (c) your training,” Gustav replied. Gustav checked Elias’s equipment once more and made sure everything was ready. Elias finally decided to face his fear. “Three, two, one… jump!” Elias jumped out of the plane, and Gustav followed right behind him. Elias suddenly felt (d) his stomach drop, and he screamed as the wind rushed past him.

(D)
Elias opened his parachute just as he had practiced, and Gustav opened his own shortly after. Elias moved down through the air, with Gustav staying nearby. Finally, they landed safely in a snow-covered field. Elias stood up, still excited by what had just happened. “We did it!” Gustav shouted, raising his hand. Elias gave (e) him a high-five. “I’ve always loved beautiful views from high places, and this was the best experience ever!” Elias said. Gustav gave him a big thumbs-up and said, “See? You were braver than you thought.”

When discussing learners’ control of their own learning, scholars often emphasize different factors. Some argue that self-efficacy provides the motivational fuel for learning. When students believe they can succeed, they are more likely to take on challenging tasks, persist through difficulty, and recover from setbacks. Other scholars view self-regulation as the operational system that directs learning. Planning, monitoring performance, and evaluating progress help learners use effort effectively. Just as fuel cannot move a vehicle without a system to direct it, a control system is useless without energy. Therefore, efficient learning requires the motivational energy supplied by self-efficacy and the guidance provided by self-regulation. Without self-regulation, effort may produce little progress, while self-regulatory strategies without sufficient self-efficacy may not be sustained consistently.

21. 밑줄 친 lose sight of the window가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은? [3점]

You tend to use wealth to signal to the world that you are worthy of being liked and admired. In reality, however, those other people often don't admire you, not because they don't think wealth is admirable, but because they use your wealth as a benchmark for their own desire to be liked and admired. They are not impressed with your possessions as much as you are. But you can hardly blame them, because you do the exact same thing. When you see someone driving a nice car, you rarely think, "Wow, the person driving that car is cool." Instead, you think, "If I had that car, people would think I am cool." In this mental process, the actual owner of the wealth completely disappears. You are using their expensive items as a blank canvas to paint your own picture of social success. You aren't really paying attention to the person who bought the item; you are just imagining a future version of yourself. Their fancy belongings don't make you respect the owner. They act as a mirror, showing your own wish to be admired. In other words, you lose sight of the window.
choices: fail to pursue your social success by paying attention to others
admit that luxury goods reflect the owner's desire to be admired
view material wealth as having little social value
stop using others' belongings as a standard for your own purchase
see your fascination with others' wealth as projecting your ideal self

22. 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?

Employees are often promoted because they perform their current jobs exceptionally well. At first glance, this seems like a reasonable way to reward strong performance and improve organizational performance. However, success in one position does not necessarily predict success in the next. Higher positions frequently require a different set of skills. For example, an outstanding salesperson may be promoted to sales manager, only to find that coaching employees, resolving conflicts, and planning strategy demand abilities unrelated to selling. According to the Peter Principle, employees continue to be promoted based on their success in their existing roles until they reach a position where they are no longer competent. As a result, even capable workers may ultimately end up in positions for which they are poorly suited. Rather than treating promotion solely as a reward for past performance, organizations should evaluate whether employees possess the skills needed for the positions they are expected to fill.

23. 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?

Driven by a collective desire to escape the standardized environments of mass tourism, contemporary travelers increasingly seek the genuine realities of local life. This pursuit of deep cultural immersion draws them away from artificial resorts and into remote villages, hidden alleyways, and untouched traditional communities. What begins as an earnest attempt to witness an authentic existence inevitably sets a subtle mechanism of commercialization in motion. As the demand for these raw experiences surges, local residents gradually adapt their traditional lifestyles to capitalize on this new demand. Spontaneous daily rituals are intentionally altered for tourist consumption, and modest local establishments expand into profit-driven venues, transforming lived reality into a meticulously staged performance. The passionate pursuit to capture a culture in its original state directly accelerates its artificialization, leaving visitors to consume a mere illusion instead of the authenticity they initially set out to discover.

24. 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?

Artificial illumination has undeniably revolutionized modern society, extending human activities and economic productivity well past sunset. Urban environments bathed in a constant glow represent a triumph over darkness, providing economic benefits and around-the-clock convenience. However, this relentless exposure to artificial light poses a profound threat to human biology. Throughout evolutionary history, our bodies have developed to operate on a delicate internal timer that governs vital functions, ranging from hormonal regulation to cellular repair, and critically relies on the complete darkness of our sleep to reset and synchronize itself properly. When artificial glare intrudes upon these unlit hours, it tricks the brain into suppressing the essential hormones necessary for restorative rest. Consequently, the absence of this crucial phase severely disrupts our biological machinery. The very brightness that fuels our modern efficiency is quietly dismantling the physiological rhythm required for human well-being.

choices: Artificial Light: The Ultimate Key to Unlocking Modern Efficiency

26. Elizabeth Blackwell에 관한 다음 글의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?

Elizabeth Blackwell was a pioneering physician who was born in Bristol, England, in 1821. When she was eleven years old, her family moved to the United States and eventually settled in Cincinnati. After the death of a close friend, she decided to pursue a career in medicine, despite being told that it was an impossible goal for a woman at the time. She was repeatedly rejected by medical schools before finally being accepted by Geneva Medical College in New York. In 1849, she graduated at the top of her class, becoming the first woman to earn a medical degree in America. She and other doctors co-founded a hospital dedicated to caring for women and children in 1857. She later returned to England and, in 1875, became a professor at the London School of Medicine for Women. She continued to advocate for medical education for women until her death in 1910.

Science deals with statements that are verified through experimentation. An experiment can be defined as controlled observation. Information is both gained and lost in ① laboratory experimentation. On the positive side, the experimenter is able to systematically examine a number of different conditions and their effect on learning because the situation is ② controlled. On the negative side, the laboratory creates an artificial situation that is much ③ different from the circumstances under which learning would actually occur. This always brings into question how information gained in the laboratory is related to learning situations outside the laboratory. Some researchers feel that ④ combining naturalistic observation and laboratory experimentation is best. That is, one could make initial observations in the field, examine them in greater detail in the laboratory. This approach is advantageous because it allows researchers to secure the precision of a controlled environment without ⑤ maintaining the real-world validity of their findings.

31. Our brains do not record what we see, hear, and experience, nor is memory a simple playback of a recording. The actual way human memory functions is closer to a little old man living inside your skull who tells you stories based on past experiences. Every time he recites one of these stories, he adapts it by leaving out minor details and filling in others that sound plausible, which means the narrative in your head may differ slightly from what actually happened. He does this because processing memories into forms he considers more rational and useful makes him handle them better. And for the most part, this old man's strategy really works; for our memory system to function properly, this editing and compression process is essential. Without this ____________ reconstruction, the immense volume of raw sensory data would overwhelm our cognitive capacity. In short, our internal storyteller isn't trying to deceive us; rather, he is an editor, trimming away the noisy extras so we can focus on what truly matters.

32. It is important to recognize that a formal knowledge of logic has played a significant role in shaping the most brilliant scientific discoveries. What is surprising is that such logical mastery grows out of a long-accumulated intuition that precedes conscious analysis. The pioneers who achieved these remarkable breakthroughs distinguished themselves by the intuitive, almost unconscious way of thinking — the same unstudied spontaneity that once allowed Jourdain to create prose. Just as Jourdain cried out, “Good heavens! For more than forty years I have been speaking prose without knowing it,” he exposed how the form of his prose rested on an intuition he never consciously recognized. Thus, it is also important to realize that if, in reading the work of great scientific pioneers such as Galileo, Kepler, Newton, Faraday, and Liebig, we first become absorbed in the rules we encounter and fail to find the unspoken patterns of their thought from which those rules originally emerged, we may be converted into mere commentators on their finished work. A proper reading of their work requires that we ____________. [3점]
choices: trace their discoveries back to the logical rules they followed
find our intuitive sense to become interpreters rather than commentators
focus on their intuitive thinking to recognize the limit of formal logic
distinguish among their intuitive patterns underlying the discoveries
search for their implicit habits of mind that gave rise to the discoveries

33. Suppose you are walking along a familiar woodland path and come to a fork yielding two equally convenient routes. As you begin to head toward the left, you notice an elaborate spider's web that you will inevitably destroy if you proceed. Assuming all other conditions are equal, should you change your direction to the right? This simple choice of altering your path fundamentally raises a profound ethical question: might a creature as primitive as a spider be endowed with moral status worthy of human consideration? Eastern philosophical traditions, which conceptualize the universe as an intricate web of mutual interdependence between humanity and lower organisms, would answer affirmatively. From this perspective, extending respect to the lowest life forms is a natural acknowledgment of universal harmony. Many in the modern West, by contrast, rooted in a tradition that views human existence as entirely independent of lower organisms, criticize as mere sentimentality the idea that insects deserve moral consideration, asserting that extending ethical deliberation to a spider is ____________.

* fork: 갈림길
choices: a misplaced concern for the spider's ecological significance
an irrational impulse to seek harmony with primitive creatures
a failure to distinguish spiders from inferior species
excessive emphasis on human independence from lower organisms
an approach incompatible with the concept of the web of life

problems.text: 34. Modernism as the prevailing standard of its time judged what is right or wrong based on a firm belief in strict rules that makes its outcome obvious and predictable. As the world witnessed how the blind faith in such strict rules led to the mass destruction of the World Wars, the belief in predictable outcomes gave way to the recognition that the world is actually uncertain and we are simply here in this world. As a result, all proclamations of modernist rules — after one color, this other color; after this line, that line — cease with ____________. On a postmodern canvas, an artist no longer started to follow a strict formula to paint a "correct" picture, where one color or line had to logically dictate the next. With no fixed result to reach at the end, the art focuses solely on the happening itself — the spontaneous physical act of brushing or splashing paint at that very moment. For artists like Newman, artistic philosophy does not reside in clear there, in another world, or another time, but in this: in that something happens. [3점]
choices: the embrace of spontaneous actions as an expression of another world
the reinforcement of strict rules that guarantee predictable outcomes
the abandonment of the happening itself in pursuit of fixed results
the awareness of the uncertain present experience that replaces formulas
the revival of absolute standards dictating the correct path of art

36. Theoretical linguists have frequently drawn on lexicography. They utilize comprehensive dictionaries as foundational tools to identify the specific features of vocabulary and establish structural frameworks for how words operate within a system.

(A) Lexicography has served the real-life needs of written communication between members of human communities using different languages or different varieties of one language. This practical aim is clearly reflected in the vast range of different dictionary types designed to respond to the different needs and interests of different users.

(B) Within the academic context, dictionaries confine their functions to the rigid boundaries of pure linguistic inquiry. Having said that, serving the needs of the scholars primarily is not an end in itself.

(C) By providing them with the appropriate vocabulary and usage guidelines for communication, lexicography has established itself as a general-purpose resource for the wider public. It has even made mutual understanding possible even among members from entirely different communities.

* lexicography: 사전편찬학

Natural selection does not require a species to be absolutely perfect. What appears to be perfection may be so only under certain conditions.

(A) Nature continues to select the sting of the honey bee as a highly effective weapon to protect the colony, even though it comes with a serious cost: its small hooks may leave the sting stuck in the skin of certain animals and sometimes cause the bee's death.
(B) Thus, no species can be regarded as absolutely perfect, since its apparent perfection depends on the other species with which it competes. What matters instead is whether a biological structure provides an overall evolutionary advantage that outweighs its limitations, meaning that even an imperfect feature can be favored by natural selection.
(C) The native species of New Zealand, for instance, had long survived and reproduced successfully before European plants and animals arrived; but many of them began to yield once these newcomers were introduced, as the new competition placed them at a competitive disadvantage. [3점]

When moving faster to capture moving prey or to escape its own predators, another visual strategy not based on background can be effective.

Avoiding detection or recognition is especially difficult for predators that must move through changing surroundings in search of food. The mimic octopus offers a striking example of how this problem can be solved without relying on a single visual strategy. ( ① ) When foraging for prey at low speeds, it adopts a coloration that matches the surrounding background, reducing the chance that either prey or predators will detect it. ( ② ) This method works well in providing visual protection while movement is limited, because the animal can continue to resemble the particular surface over which it is traveling. ( ③ ) The octopus maintains visual protection by shifting to a form of deception, changing its body form to resemble animals such as flatfish, lionfish, or banded sea snakes. ( ④ ) This change in strategy reflects the reduced success of background matching when the animal moves rapidly through varied environments. ( ⑤ ) The mimic octopus therefore adjusts its appearance to the demands created by its own movement.

Instead, what looks like a set of rules has taken shape little by little as builders have retained solutions suited to local climate, available materials, and ways of life.

Unlike large-scale urban buildings, which are typically constructed according to detailed plans and predetermined specifications, traditional houses in a region are not bound to a strict set of design rules. ( ① ) Yet villages in the region often come to share recognizable features, such as similar roof slopes, window sizes, courtyard arrangements, and choices of building materials. ( ② ) Recurring design elements should not be understood as instructions that builders first received and then followed. ( ③ ) Such similarities carry no implication that individual houses in the region are built according to a uniform pattern. ( ④ ) A steep roof might be used repeatedly because it sheds heavy rain efficiently, and thick walls could continue to be adopted because their insulation helps keep indoor temperatures stable. 40. 다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

When movements are visible, we can copy them; we can just do what we see. However, this imitation is not necessarily something we choose to do. The human mirror neuron system unconsciously replicates and activates the same action representations simply by observing another person's behavior, as if performing those actions itself. For introverts, this automatic simulation can create internal tension when the behavior they observe conflicts with their own preferred way of acting. Consider introverts observing behavior they would never engage in ― like loud, overly persistent self-promotion in a crowded room. While the mirror system automatically simulates what they see, their conscious self rejects the behavior, actively resisting the action. To prevent themselves from actually executing these unwanted actions, their cognitive control network must constantly counter the mirror system's automatic replication. This continuous collision between neural activation and conscious inhibition may force their mental control mechanisms to make an extremely demanding effort, with no energy left to even respond to simple social interactions.

↓

Because our imitation of others' actions is not necessarily (A), the continuous attempt by an introvert's brain to suppress this automatic neural simulation may cause cognitive (B) as it struggles to inhibit unwanted behavior.
